title: Vossius: the Latria–Dulia split is not scriptural or classical, yet not wholly rejected
source_text: XX. Quibus similia tradit Gerardus Joannes Vossius in Thesibus Theologicis. Discrimen, inquit, vocabulorum λατρείας & δουλείας, quo illa uni Deo, haec creaturis etiam dicitur convenire, nec in Scripturis sacris, nec in scriptoribus classicis observatur: ut etiam Valla, Vives, aliique agnoscunt. Imo δουλείας vox, nisi eam metaphorice sumamus, Sanctis minus quam Deo competit: quia ratione cultus religiosi, non creaturae, sed Dei δοῦλοι sumus: quemadmodum ex Pontificiis Pereziius agnovit, frustra improbante Bellarmino. Nihilominus eos qui distinctionem hanc probant minime improbamus: partim quia vitanda est viro prudenti omnis ὁμωνυμία; partim quia nec inutile videtur, si cultibus toto genere differentibus, qualis est Dei & creaturae, ad homonymiam vitandam diversa imponantur nomina: partim denique quia nec ab ea abhorruit Augustinus. Nec idcirco praevaricamur, vel Pontificiorum causam juvamus quicquam; quia (ut Calvinus hac de distinctione agens agnoscit) de re non de voce quaestio est. Nempe hoc est quod in Pontificiis damnamus, quod cultum suum Deo illibatum non servant, sed divinum honorem magna parte transcribunt Sanctis. Appendice ad disputationem decimam, quae est quarta de Invocatione Sanctorum.
pass_a_gloss: Gerard Joannes Vossius hands down similar things in his Theological Theses. The difference, he says, of the words latreia and douleia, by which the former is said to suit God alone and the latter creatures also, is observed neither in the sacred Scriptures nor in the classical writers, as Valla, Vives, and others also acknowledge. Indeed the word douleia, unless we take it metaphorically, suits the Saints less than God, because by reason of religious cult we are slaves not of a creature but of God, as Perezius among the Pontificals acknowledged, Bellarmine disapproving in vain. Nevertheless we by no means disapprove those who approve this distinction: partly because a prudent man must avoid all homonymy; partly because it does not seem useless, if different names are imposed on cults differing in their whole kind, such as that of God and of the creature, to avoid homonymy; and partly finally because Augustine did not shrink from it. Nor do we on that account prevaricate or help the Pontificals' cause at all, because, as Calvin acknowledges when treating this distinction, the question is about the thing, not about the word. For this is what we condemn in the Pontificals, that they do not keep their cult of God undiminished, but transfer divine honor in great part to the Saints. In the appendix to the tenth disputation, which is the fourth on the Invocation of the Saints.
pass_b_english: Vossius says neither Scripture nor the classics observe a Latria for God and a Dulia for creatures, as Valla and Vives also grant.
Taken strictly, douleia fits God more than the Saints, since religious service makes us God's servants; Perezius saw this, and Bellarmine's objection fails.
He still does not condemn the distinction, as a guard against ambiguous names, and because Augustine did not refuse it.
The quarrel with Rome is the thing, not the word: they do not leave God's cult whole, but hand a large part of divine honor to the Saints.

lemmas.gloss: about the thing, not about the word

choices.why: The allowed use of the names is to prevent one word covering two kinds of cult.
